slides.text:
A CLI starts as one file and grows. Cobra projects settle on a shape: a thin `main.go` and one file per command inside a `cmd` folder.

The snippet is a folder sketch, not Go.
slides.code:
myapp/
    main.go
    cmd/
        root.go
        greet.go
        version.go

slides.text: The editor here holds a single `main.go`, so each file becomes a function: a constructor for the root, one per command, and a short `main`. You will go from global commands to constructors, pass flags and settings down, and finish with a small whole CLI.

A global `rootCmd` is built once, when the program starts, and an `init` function can add to it. Every part of the program then shares that single command.

A constructor is a function that returns a new command on each call.

The snippet is pseudo code.
slides.code:
global style:
    one command, made at startup

constructor style:
    each call makes a new command

slides.text:
With constructors, each command gets its own function and the root decides what it contains. Nothing is shared by accident.

`Commands()` returns the subcommands a command holds, as a slice.

exercises.title: A global root command
exercises.guide: Start with the common layout: a global root command and an `init` that wires a subcommand.

chunks.guide: A package-level variable holds the root command.

notes.text: One command, created when the program starts.

chunks.guide: A second global holds the subcommand.
Register the subcommand before `main` runs.

notes.text: Runs by itself, before main starts.

chunks.guide: `main` only has to run the root.
chunks.text: rootCmd.Execute()

exercises.title: The cost of a global command
exercises.guide: Pick the problem this code has if the program needs a second, clean root command.
options: init runs after main, so the command is empty
Every part of the program shares that one command
A global command cannot have subcommands
exercises.explanation: `rootCmd` is created once and every file that touches it changes the same value, so you cannot get a fresh copy.

exercises.title: A constructor for the root
exercises.guide: Replace the global with a function that builds a new root command on every call.

chunks.guide: The function returns the command instead of keeping it in a variable.

notes.text: Every call builds a brand new command.

chunks.guide: Call the constructor, then run what it returns.
chunks.text:
root := newRootCmd()
    root.Execute()

exercises.title: Hand back the root
exercises.guide: Fill the gaps: return the new command, build the root with the constructor and run it.

exercises.title: One function per command
exercises.guide: Give the subcommand its own constructor and let the root collect it.

chunks.guide: Same shape as the root constructor, for one subcommand.
The root builds itself and adds its subcommand.

notes.text: The root only asks the constructor for the command.

exercises.title: Two roots
exercises.explanation: Each call builds a separate command, so the subcommand added to `a` is not in `b`. With a global `rootCmd` they would be the same command.

slides.text:
Keep what a command needs next to it. Flag values live in the constructor, and several of them can go into one options struct. The real work sits in plain functions, and shared settings arrive as parameters.

The snippet is pseudo code.
slides.code:
newGreetCmd(settings):
    values = this command's flags
    when run: greet(values, settings)

exercises.title: A flag inside its command
exercises.guide: Keep a flag and its value inside the constructor of the command that uses them.

chunks.guide: The value of the flag is a local variable of the constructor.

notes.text: No other command can see this value.

exercises.title: Logic outside the command
exercises.guide: Write the greeting as a plain function over an options struct, with no cobra in it.

chunks.guide: A struct will hold everything the greeting needs.
The logic only reads the options. A command can call it later.
Call it with options built by hand.
chunks.text:
opts := greetOptions{name: "Ana", shout: true}
    fmt.Println(greet(opts))

exercises.title: Flags into the struct
exercises.guide: Bind the flags of the command straight into the fields of the options struct.

chunks.guide: The command only reads its flags and calls `greet`.

notes.text: The flag writes straight into the field.

chunks.guide: Add the command to a root and run it.

exercises.title: Bind to the options
exercises.guide: Fill the gaps: the method of a text flag, the struct variable and what the constructor hands back.

exercises.title: What opts is for
exercises.guide: What does the options struct do in this command?
options: It collects the values of all the command's flags
It stores the name and help text of the command
It shares the flags with every subcommand
It checks that the user gave the flags
exercises.explanation: Each flag writes into one field, so the command's whole input travels in one value that plain functions can take.

exercises.title: Dependencies as parameters
exercises.guide: Hand the greeting to the command as a parameter instead of reading a global.

chunks.guide: A small struct for what the commands share.
The constructor takes the config it needs.

notes.text: The command gets what it needs as a parameter.

chunks.guide: The root builds the config once and passes it down.

slides.text: `main` should do almost nothing: build the root and run it, as you have since the first modules. Everything else is in constructors, which in a real project would each get a file, so adding a command never touches `main`.

exercises.title: Add a command, keep main
exercises.guide: Add a second command: only constructors change, `main` stays as it is.

chunks.guide: The new command gets its own constructor.
The root lists both commands.

notes.text: The only line that changes when a command is added

exercises.title: Wire the root
exercises.guide: Fill the gaps: the field that names the root, the method that collects its commands and what the constructor hands back.

exercises.title: Where the commands live
exercises.guide: The CLI grows to ten commands. Where does each constructor go?
options: All in main.go, in one long file
Each in its own package with its own main
Each in a file of cmd, next to root.go
exercises.explanation: One file per command inside the `cmd` package, with `root.go` wiring them. `cmd` is a separate package from `main`, so what `main.go` calls (like `NewRootCmd`) needs a capital letter to be exported.

exercises.title: The whole layout
exercises.guide: Put it all together: a version variable, the commands and one place that wires them.

chunks.guide: A package variable for the release number.

notes.text: A build flag can set the real release number.

chunks.text: var version = "dev"

chunks.guide: The one place that lists every command. The two constructors are already in the file.
